cases.abstract: Imitation policies trained on a small set of wrist-camera demonstrations can fail when execution drifts beyond the observed trajectories. DMD expands training coverage by synthesizing nearby camera views and assigning each an action from its perturbed pose toward a later expert pose. A pretrained, pose-conditioned diffusion model is adapted using task demonstrations, task-agnostic play, or both; reconstructed camera poses connect view generation to action labeling. Later-frame targets reduce the risk of backward commands when a generated viewpoint has already passed the immediate successor. Robot experiments cover pushing, stacking, pouring, and shirt hanging. With 24 pushing demonstrations and a generator trained on task and play data, DMD succeeds in 10/10 trials, compared with 3/10 for behavior cloning. In cup arrangement with 1,447 demonstrations, augmentation improves a retrained Diffusion Policy from 4/25 to 16/25 successes on five unseen cups in a new environment; both policies receive identically cropped, rectified images. These comparisons support off-trajectory supervision for both regression and diffusion policies, including beyond the low-data regime. Recovery labels assume recoverable deviations and cannot undo irreversible events such as spilling beans.
cases.methods: Each synthesized view needs an action target consistent with its displaced camera pose, rather than the unmodified source label. DMD uses structure from motion to reconstruct demonstration poses and fine-tunes a pretrained diffusion model on image pairs and their relative transforms. The model then renders a nearby virtual camera view for a requested displacement. Composing the inverse displacement with the transform from the source pose to a future expert pose yields the movement from the virtual pose to that target. If the virtual pose has passed the next expert frame, however, targeting that frame commands backward motion. DMD instead targets the third subsequent frame: directional-error improvement plateaus near this offset, whereas larger offsets discard more terminal frames. Training on original and generated pairs thus adds supervision for returning from local deviations toward task progress, provided those states remain recoverable.
cases.results: On held-out pushing trajectories, DMD improves on standard image augmentation: median directional error is 0.328 radians, versus 0.355 for behavior cloning, when both use color jitter and horizontal flips. With 24 demonstrations and a generator trained on task and play data, robot success rises from 3/10 for behavior cloning to 10/10 for DMD. The deployment contrast is consistent with accumulated action errors affecting outcomes, but does not isolate that mechanism. With eight demonstrations, DMD still succeeds in 8/10 trials versus 2/10 for behavior cloning; its generator uses separate play data, so eight demonstrations are not the entire training-data budget. Benefits also persist with a larger dataset: after 1,447 cup-arrangement demonstrations, augmentation improves a retrained Diffusion Policy from 4/25 to 16/25 successes on five unseen cups in a new lab, using matched starts and identical cropped, rectified inputs. This supports utility under the tested object and environment shift, despite nine failures. The corrective supervision remains conditional on recoverable states; returning to an expert camera pose cannot restore spilled contents.
cases.notes: Retained corrective supervision as the central contribution. Abstract sentences 2-4 and Methods explain how a displaced view receives a transform-based target (III-C; Fig. 5), with later targets reducing rather than eliminating overshooting. Results contrasts augmentation with BC and separates policy demonstrations from generator play data (Tables I-II). The large-data comparison uses retrained, cropped/rectified Diffusion Policy inputs and matched starts (IV-E; Table V). Pouring comparisons remain omitted because they used separate randomized A/B tests with different BC outcomes. Trial fractions are descriptive, not population guarantees.

cases.abstract: Fine bimanual manipulation requires demonstrations of delicate coordination and policies that limit error accumulation during high-frequency execution. ALOHA provides an open-source teleoperation platform within a $20,000 budget, directly coupling leader and follower joints to avoid inverse-kinematics failures near singularities. Action Chunking with Transformers (ACT) predicts sequences of joint targets to shorten the effective decision horizon. Overlapping predictions are updated every step and combined for the same execution time, retaining frequent feedback while smoothing transitions; conditional variational training models variation in human demonstrations. Evaluation spans two simulated and six physical tasks, with 50 demonstrations per physical task except threading, which uses 100. In 25 trials per physical task with one training seed, reported final-stage rates for ACT are 88% for opening an upright slider bag and 96% for battery insertion, while four tuned imitation baselines report zero on either final stage. Threading reaches only 20%, showing that coordinated predictions leave difficult visual-localization problems unresolved. Separately, six participants complete threading and cup separation faster at 50 Hz than at 5 Hz, supporting high-frequency input updates in human teleoperation.
cases.methods: ACT treats each observation as the start of a sequence of future joint targets for both arms. Demonstrations pair follower joint positions and four camera views with leader joint targets; using leader targets preserves the command differences through which the position controller applies contact forces. A transformer predicts the whole chunk to model short stretches of temporally dependent behavior and reduce the effective decision horizon. Waiting for each chunk to finish would delay new feedback and can produce abrupt transitions. Instead, the policy is queried every step, and overlapping predictions are exponentially weighted only when they target the same execution time. This smooths transitions without mixing actions for neighboring times. Conditional variational training represents variation in demonstrated sequences with reconstruction and Gaussian-prior regularization. At inference, its encoder is discarded and the latent variable set to zero, yielding deterministic predictions from current observations.
cases.results: With temporal ensembling disabled, increasing ACT's chunk length from one to 100 actions raises mean simulation success from 1% to 44% across two tasks trained with either scripted or human demonstrations. Longer chunks slightly reduce success, suggesting a tradeoff between horizon reduction, responsiveness, and sequence-modeling difficulty. Conditional variational training addresses a different issue: removing it lowers success on human demonstrations from 35.3% to 2%, averaged across the two simulated tasks, while changing little for deterministic scripted data. Its observed benefit is therefore concentrated in the human-data setting. Comparing separately tuned configurations, temporal ensembling improves ACT by 3.3 percentage points but lowers VINN's success. The hardware study separately tests leader-input frequency: six participants average 20 rather than 33 seconds for threading at 50 versus 5 Hz, with follower commands maintained at 50 Hz. These findings do not eliminate the autonomous threading failure: only 20% of trials succeed despite 100 demonstrations, with premature grasping and missed insertion exposing remaining visual-localization difficulties.
cases.notes: Abstract retains ALOHA and ACT as co-contributions; Methods links joint-target chunks to feedback-preserving overlap (IV-A-C). Results separates chunking, human-data CVAE gains, and separately tuned ensemble outcomes, including VINN's adverse result (Fig. 9a-c). Human timing evidence remains distinct from policy success; Appendix E keeps follower commands at 50 Hz under 5 Hz leader sampling. Table II reports 92% grasping, 96% pinching, and 88% opening for Slide Ziploc. Final-stage rates are retained without inferring joint completion; query how stages were counted. Main physical evaluations use one seed and 25 trials, not an established denominator for every ablation.
